{{Short description|Category theory}}
In [[category theory]], a '''Kleisli category''' is a [[category (mathematics)|category]] naturally associated to any [[monad (category theory)|monad]] ''T''. It is equivalent to the category of [[Free object|free]] [[Monad (category theory)#Algebras for a monad|''T''-algebras]]. The Kleisli category is one of two extremal solutions to the question: "''Does every monad arise from an [[Adjunction (category theory)|adjunction]]?''" The other extremal solution is the [[Eilenberg–Moore category]]. Kleisli categories are named for the mathematician [[Heinrich Kleisli]].

==Formal definition==

Let &lang;''T'', ''η'', ''μ''&rang; be a [[monad (category theory)|monad]] over a category ''C''. The '''Kleisli category''' of ''C'' is the category ''C''<sub>''T''</sub> whose objects and morphisms are given by
:<math>\begin{align}\mathrm{Obj}({\mathcal{C}_T}) &= \mathrm{Obj}({\mathcal{C}}), \\
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}_T}(X,Y) &= \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X,TY).\end{align}</math>
That is, every morphism ''f: X &rarr; T Y'' in ''C'' (with codomain ''TY'') can also be regarded as a morphism in ''C''<sub>''T''</sub> (but with codomain ''Y''). Composition of morphisms in ''C''<sub>''T''</sub> is given by
:<math>g\circ_T f = \mu_Z \circ Tg \circ f : X \to T Y \to T^2 Z \to T Z</math>
where ''f: X &rarr; T Y'' and ''g: Y &rarr; T Z''. The identity morphism is given by the monad unit ''&eta;'':
:<math>\mathrm{id}_X = \eta_X</math>.

An alternative way of writing this, which clarifies the category in which each object lives, is used by [[Saunders Mac Lane|MacLane]].<ref name=macLane>{{cite book| last= Mac Lane | date=1998|title= Categories for the Working Mathematician|page=147}}</ref>  We use very slightly different notation for this presentation.  Given the same monad and category <math>C</math> as above, we associate with each object <math>X</math> in&nbsp;<math>C</math> a new object <math>X_T</math>, and for each morphism <math>f\colon X\to TY</math> in&nbsp;<math>C</math> a morphism <math>f^*\colon X_T\to Y_T</math>.  Together, these objects and morphisms form our category <math>C_T</math>, where we define composition, also called '''Kleisli composition''', by
:<math>g^*\circ_T f^* = (\mu_Z \circ Tg \circ f)^*.</math>
Then the identity morphism in <math>C_T</math>, the '''Kleisli identity''', is
:<math>\mathrm{id}_{X_T} = (\eta_X)^*.</math>

==Extension operators and Kleisli triples==

Composition of Kleisli arrows can be expressed succinctly by means of the ''extension operator'' (–)<sup>#</sup> : Hom(''X'', ''TY'') &rarr; Hom(''TX'', ''TY''). Given a monad &lang;''T'', ''η'', ''μ''&rang; over a category ''C'' and a morphism ''f'' : ''X'' &rarr; ''TY'' let
:<math>f^\sharp = \mu_Y\circ Tf.</math>
Composition in the Kleisli category ''C''<sub>''T''</sub> can then be written
:<math>g\circ_T f = g^\sharp \circ f.</math>
The extension operator satisfies the identities:
:<math>\begin{align}\eta_X^\sharp &= \mathrm{id}_{TX}\\
f^\sharp\circ\eta_X &= f\\
(g^\sharp\circ f)^\sharp &= g^\sharp \circ f^\sharp\end{align}</math>
where ''f'' : ''X'' &rarr; ''TY'' and ''g'' : ''Y'' &rarr; ''TZ''. It follows trivially from these properties that Kleisli composition is associative and that ''&eta;''<sub>''X''</sub> is the identity.

In fact, to give a monad is to give a ''Kleisli triple'' &lang;''T'', ''&eta;'', (–)<sup>#</sup>&rang;, i.e. 
* A function <math>T\colon \mathrm{ob}(C)\to \mathrm{ob}(C)</math>;
* For each object <math>A</math> in <math>C</math>, a morphism <math>\eta_A\colon A\to T(A)</math>;
* For each morphism <math>f\colon A\to T(B)</math> in <math>C</math>, a morphism <math>f^\sharp\colon T(A)\to T(B)</math>
such that the above three equations for extension operators are satisfied.

==Kleisli adjunction==

Kleisli categories were originally defined in order to show that every monad arises from an adjunction. That construction is as follows.

Let &lang;''T'', ''η'', ''μ''&rang; be a monad over a category ''C'' and let ''C''<sub>''T''</sub> be the associated Kleisli category. Using Mac Lane's notation mentioned in the “Formal definition” section above, define a functor ''F'':&nbsp;''C''&nbsp;&rarr;&nbsp;''C''<sub>''T''</sub> by
:<math>FX = X_T\;</math>
:<math>F(f\colon X \to Y) = (\eta_Y \circ f)^*</math>
and a functor ''G'' : ''C''<sub>''T''</sub> &rarr; ''C'' by
:<math>GY_T = TY\;</math>
:<math>G(f^*\colon X_T \to Y_T) = \mu_Y \circ Tf\;</math>
One can show that ''F'' and ''G'' are indeed functors and that ''F'' is left adjoint to ''G''. The counit of the adjunction is given by
:<math>\varepsilon_{Y_T} = (\mathrm{id}_{TY})^* : (TY)_T \to Y_T.</math>
Finally, one can show that ''T'' = ''GF'' and ''&mu;'' = ''G&epsilon;F'' so that &lang;''T'', ''η'', ''μ''&rang; is the monad associated to the adjunction &lang;''F'', ''G'', ''η'', ''ε''&rang;.

===Showing that ''GF'' = ''T''===
For any object ''X'' in category ''C'':
: <math>\begin{align}
(G \circ F)(X) &= G(F(X)) \\
&= G(X_T) \\
&= TX.
\end{align}</math>

For any <math>f : X \to Y</math> in category ''C'':
: <math>\begin{align}
(G \circ F)(f) &= G(F(f)) \\
&= G((\eta_Y \circ f)^*) \\
&= \mu_Y \circ T(\eta_Y \circ f) \\
&= \mu_Y \circ T\eta_Y \circ Tf \\
&= \text{id}_{TY} \circ Tf \\
&= Tf.
\end{align}</math>
Since <math>(G \circ F)(X) = TX</math> is true for any object ''X'' in ''C'' and <math>(G \circ F)(f) = Tf</math> is true for any morphism ''f'' in ''C'', then <math>G \circ F = T</math>. [[Q.E.D.]]
